title: How do you film UGC when you live with other people?
description: Filming UGC in a shared house: how to agree quiet times with housemates, pick a corner that works, and check every frame so their lives stay out of it.
short_answer: To film UGC when you live with other people, agree set filming slots with them, pick one corner you can reset quickly, and check every frame before you send it. Ask before anyone or anything of theirs appears on camera, and plan your shots so a door opening or a kettle boiling costs you one take, not the whole day.

sections.heading: How do you agree filming time with the people you live with?

blocks.text: Agree a few regular filming slots with your housemates in advance, so they know when to keep quiet and you know when to film.

Grabbing whatever quiet moment appears tends to end in frustration on both sides. A slot you have asked for in advance is easier for other people to respect than a sudden request to be quiet. Keep the ask small and specific, and offer something back. Wording you can adapt:

items: I have a filming job for [PRODUCT] this week. Could I have the living room quiet on [DATE] in the morning?
I will put a note on my door when I am recording, and take it down the moment I finish.
If you need the kitchen during that time, just knock and I will pause.
Happy to swap: if you need the place quiet for a call one day, tell me and I will keep clear.

blocks.text: Before you agree a delivery date with a [brand](/glossary/#brand), check it against these slots. [What questions should you ask a brand before you start filming?](/blog/questions-to-ask-before-filming-ugc/) helps you pin down the timing before you promise anything at home.

sections.heading: Where in a shared home should you film?

blocks.text: Film in the space you control most, such as your own room, and make a second shared spot work only for the shots that need it.

Your bedroom is the one place where nobody walks in to make toast, so set up a corner there that you can return to every time. A wall, a shelf you keep tidy and a window to one side give you a backdrop you can reset in minutes. Use the kitchen or bathroom only when the [script](/glossary/#script) needs that room, and film those shots first in your slot, while the house is still quiet. Mapping the shots before the day helps here: write a short [shot list](/glossary/#shot-list) that groups everything by room, so you only claim each shared space once. Reading the brief the way [turning a brand brief into a script](/blog/brief-to-script/) describes makes it clear which locations are required and which are up to you.

table_rows: Talking to camera, close-ups, most product shots
Your bed, laundry and anything personal on the walls
Food, drink and cleaning products in use
Other people's food, notes on the fridge, the fridge hum
Other people's products on the shelf and in the mirror
Post with names on it and the front door in shot

sections.heading: How do you keep your housemates out of the video?

blocks.text: Check the whole frame, including mirrors and windows, and ask before anyone or anything of theirs appears on camera.

A video for a brand can be seen far beyond your own followers, so treat everyone you live with as someone who has not agreed to be in it. Before each setup, do a slow pan of the frame on your phone and look for these:

items: Faces or bodies in the background, including a reflection in a mirror, window or a dark screen.
Photos, artwork or names that belong to someone else.
Letters, parcels or anything with an address on it.
Other people's belongings, especially products from other companies, which the brand may not want next to its own.
Voices in the audio track, which can be just as identifying as a face.

blocks.text: If a housemate is willing to appear, for a dialogue scene or a hand in shot, ask them plainly and tell them where the video will be used. Then check with the brand that it is happy for another person to appear, and follow what the brief says. If anyone has doubts, leave them out.

sections.heading: How do you handle noise you cannot control?

blocks.text: Plan for interruptions by keeping each line short, so a slammed door means retaking one sentence instead of the whole video.

Film one [beat](/glossary/#beat) at a time, pausing between them, and keep rolling for a moment after you finish speaking. When a noise lands, stop, wait for it to pass and repeat the line from the start, so the edit has a clean version. Soft furnishings in your room help the sound too, and [how do you get clear audio in a UGC video?](/blog/ugc-audio/) goes further on that. Shots with no speaking, like product close-ups and hands, can go in the noisier part of the day, because you can add the voice or music later. [What B-roll should you film for a UGC video?](/blog/ugc-b-roll/) lists those shots.

sections.heading: What should you check before you send the files?

blocks.text: Watch every clip once with the sound up and once frame by frame at the edges, looking only for things that belong to other people.

It is easy to miss a housemate's reflection or a voice in the next room when you are focused on your own delivery. A separate pass that looks only at the background catches what the first one misses. If you find something, crop it, cut it or reshoot it in your next slot rather than hoping nobody notices. Light also changes through the day in a shared home as curtains open and close, so if shots look mismatched, [how do you light a UGC video at home?](/blog/light-ugc-at-home/) helps you even them out next time.
